abstract: Populations declining under anthropogenic stressors, including rising temperatures and novel chemicals, may depend on rapid adaptation to persist. Yet fundamental questions remain about what promotes and constrains such evolutionary rescue. We tracked demographic, phenotypic, and genomic dynamics in a replicated outdoor evolution experiment using Drosophila under insecticide stress, and also manipulated initial maladaptation by pre-adapting a subset of populations. Half of populations without pre-adaptation went extinct and, unexpectedly, extinction was associated with a greater magnitude of phenotypic and parallel genomic adaptation. Rescue was driven by polygenic adaptation that was parallel across replicates and not predictable from genes previously implicated in insecticide resistance, with notable genomic convergence towards pre-adapted populations. Targeted intervention through pre-adaptation prevented extinction entirely, despite evidence of pleiotropic costs. Without intervention, evolutionary rescue remains contingent even with exceptionally rapid adaptation.
